title: Fictitious Forces and Non-inertial Frames: The Coriolis Force
short: Fictitious forces and the Coriolis force
lead: Take off in a jet, turn a corner in a car, or ride a merry-go-round, and you feel forces that a physicist standing on the ground says are not there at all. These fictitious forces come from a non-inertial frame of reference, and you can set one against an inertial frame. The Coriolis force then carries you from a ball slid across a merry-go-round out to the rotation of hurricanes and tropical cyclones.
objectives: Discuss the inertial frame of reference.
Discuss the non-inertial frame of reference.
Describe the effects of the Coriolis force.
summary_html:
• Rotating and accelerated frames of reference are non-inertial.
  • Fictitious forces, such as the Coriolis force, are needed to explain motion in such frames.

figures.original_caption: (a) The car driver feels herself forced to the left relative to the car when she makes a right turn. This is a fictitious force arising from the use of the car as a frame of reference. (b) In the Earth’s frame of reference, the driver moves in a straight line, obeying Newton’s first law, and the car moves to the right. There is no real force to the left on the driver relative to Earth. There is a real force to the right on the car to make it turn.

(a) A rider on a merry-go-round feels as if he is being thrown off. This fictitious force is called the centrifugal force—it explains the rider’s motion in the rotating frame of reference.  (b) In an inertial frame of reference and according to Newton’s laws, it is his inertia that carries him off and not a real force (the  unshaded rider has F_net = 0 and heads in a straight line). A real force, F_centripetal, is needed to cause a circular path.

Centrifuges use inertia to perform their task. Particles in the fluid sediment come out because their inertia carries them away from the center of rotation. The large angular velocity of the centrifuge quickens the sedimentation. Ultimately, the particles will come into contact with the test tube walls, which will then supply the centripetal force needed to make them move in a circle of constant radius.

exercises.prompt: When a toilet is flushed or a sink is drained, the water (and other material) begins to rotate about the drain on the way down. Assuming no initial rotation and a flow initially directly straight toward the drain, explain what causes the rotation and which direction it has in the northern hemisphere. (Note that this is a small effect and in most toilets the rotation is caused by directional water jets.) Would the direction of rotation reverse if water were forced up the drain?

answer.solution: Nothing gives the water its rotation at the drain; it acquires it on the way in. Each parcel of water moves over a rotating Earth, and in the northern hemisphere the Coriolis force turns any motion to the right. It turns the ball slid across the merry-go-round and the winds flowing into a low pressure the same way. Water coming in from every side turns the same way round, so the flow is counterclockwise, like a northern hemisphere hurricane. Earth’s angular velocity is small, so over a basin the effect is tiny, and the shape of the bowl or the jets usually decide the direction instead. If you forced the water up the drain, each parcel would move outward, and the same deflection to the right would turn the rotation clockwise. For the same reason, wind flowing away from a high-pressure zone circulates clockwise in the northern hemisphere.

exercises.prompt: Is there a real force that throws water from clothes during the spin cycle of a washing machine? Explain how the water is removed.

answer.solution: There is no real force throwing the water outward. The drum carries the clothes round in a circle, and to go in a circle each piece of cloth and each drop of water needs a real force pointing toward the axis. The wall of the drum supplies that force to the clothes, and the cloth supplies it to the water it holds, but a hole in the drum supplies nothing. A drop that reaches a hole has no force toward the axis, so its inertia carries it along a tangent, out through the hole. In the rotating frame of the drum, the fictitious centrifugal force accounts for the same motion, and the faster the drum spins the greater that force is. In Earth’s frame the water simply goes straight while the drum turns away from underneath it.

exercises.prompt: In one amusement park ride, riders enter a large vertical barrel and stand against the wall on its horizontal floor. The barrel is spun up and the floor drops away. Riders feel as if they are pinned to the wall by a force something like the gravitational force. This is a fictitious force sensed and used by the riders to explain events in the rotating frame of reference of the barrel. Explain in an inertial frame of reference (Earth is nearly one) what pins the riders to the wall, and identify all of the real forces acting on them.

answer.solution: In Earth’s frame nothing pins the riders outward. Three real forces act on a rider. The wall of the barrel pushes inward on them, horizontally, toward the axis. That normal force is the centripetal force, and it keeps them going round the circle instead of along the straight line their inertia would follow. Earth pulls them down with their weight. The wall also exerts friction on them along its surface, upward, and that friction holds them up once the floor drops away. So the ride must spin fast enough for the normal force, and with it the friction, to balance the weight. The riders feel their backs pressed against the wall because, by Newton’s third law, they push outward on the wall just as hard as it pushes inward on them. In the rotating frame of the barrel, the fictitious centrifugal force accounts for that sensation, and it has no physical origin at all.

exercises.prompt: A non-rotating frame of reference placed at the center of the Sun is very nearly an inertial one. Why is it not exactly an inertial frame?

answer.solution: An inertial frame is one in which all forces are real, which means a frame that is not itself accelerated. A frame at the center of the Sun and not turning is very nearly such a frame, because the Sun is so massive that the planets move it very little and because the frame does not rotate with it. It is not exactly inertial because the Sun is not free of forces. The planets pull on the Sun, so the Sun swings in a small orbit of its own about the center of mass of the solar system, and the Sun as a whole is in orbit about the center of the Milky Way, which is an acceleration toward that center. A frame carried along with the Sun is therefore accelerated, if only slightly, and to that extent it is non-inertial.
